articles.title: Compare Image Generation APIs for 7-Stage Portable Media Hiring SaaS Apps
articles.excerpt: A 7-Stage Image Artifact Contract for Portable Media Hiring SaaS When a media hiring SaaS must compare image generation APIs, the expensive mistake is treating generation as a single request that retu…
articles.body: A 7-Stage Image Artifact Contract for Portable Media Hiring SaaS When a media hiring SaaS must compare image generation APIs, the expensive mistake is treating generation as a single request that returns a URL. A candidate-scoring workflow needs a durable artifact contract: prompt intent, provider request, binary output, policy result, and rubric evidence must remain understandable after the underlying API changes. Short answer: put a provider-neutral job record in front of every image API, store the resulting bytes under your own immutable object key, and make the scoring service consume that record rather than a vendor response. Compare providers on the shape and survivability of that record first.
articles.author: FluxH91

articles.title: 7 Best Notification Infrastructure APIs in 2026 (Compared)
articles.excerpt: Every SaaS product ends up building the same notification system twice. The first version is a send_email() call inside a controller. The second one arrives six months later, when users ask for an in-…
articles.body: Every SaaS product ends up building the same notification system twice. The first version is a send_email() call inside a controller. The second one arrives six months later, when users ask for an in-app inbox, a "daily digest instead of 40 emails" setting, and a way to mute Slack alerts without muting everything. If you're: adding an in-app inbox to your product, replacing a pile of email, SMS and push calls with one API, or choosing between Knock, Novu and Courier, this comparison is for you. Short answer: pick Knock if you want the most polished developer experience with digests on the free plan. Pick Novu if you want open source (MIT) and the lowest bill. Pick SuprSend if you need WhatsApp and the widest channel list.

articles.title: I Built DTDb — An IMDb for Developer Tools
articles.excerpt: We developers have strong opinions about the tools we use every day. Vim vs. VS Code. PostgreSQL vs. MySQL. Ubuntu vs. Arch. Python vs. Go. And now, with AI coding agents becoming part of everyday dev…
articles.body: We developers have strong opinions about the tools we use every day. Vim vs. VS Code. PostgreSQL vs. MySQL. Ubuntu vs. Arch. Python vs. Go. And now, with AI coding agents becoming part of everyday development, there are even more tools to compare. But where can you actually see what developers think about these tools? There are plenty of comparison articles, sponsored rankings, benchmarks, and opinionated blog posts. But I wanted something a little different. So I built DTDb — Developer Tools Database. 👉 https://dtdb.dev What's the idea? Think of IMDb, but instead of movies, we're ranking developer tools. The concept is simple: Developers rate the tools they actually use. Tools are organized into categories. Each month, ratings are frozen into a ranking.

articles.excerpt: What I Built Ofrenda is a private, offline digital altar for families. For Día de los Muertos, families set up an ofrenda to remember the people they've lost. I took that idea further: the altar can h…
articles.body: What I Built Ofrenda is a private, offline digital altar for families. For Día de los Muertos, families set up an ofrenda to remember the people they've lost. I took that idea further: the altar can hold a person, a festival, or a ritual, because those are also what a family carries forward. Ganpati, Diwali lamp walks, a grandmother's recipe, and her voice telling a story all belong on the altar. You can record a story in the browser, upload an audio file or a video, write a story, or upload a photo. Each memory can carry its own photo and is marked as a Recipe, Ritual, Festival, or Story. Audio and video are transcribed locally. When a story isn't in English, the app keeps the original transcript and adds an English version.

articles.title: What 120,000 invented rows taught me about moving a SQL Server 2012 app to Dataverse
articles.excerpt: This is a test migration on invented records. Kove Energy is a showcase firm, not a client. I built a stand-in for an old SQL Server 2012 database, gave it the faults old databases usually have, and m…
articles.body: This is a test migration on invented records. Kove Energy is a showcase firm, not a client. I built a stand-in for an old SQL Server 2012 database, gave it the faults old databases usually have, and moved it into a Dataverse environment to see what breaks. The migration, the build and the app are real. The data is not. I am writing it up because the useful part is the failure and reconciliation evidence, not the headline row count. The setup The scenario is a home energy installer of about 15 people running a custom Windows desktop app on SQL Server 2012 Standard, on Windows Server 2012 R2. Both layers are past end of support. SQL Server 2012 is not supported on Windows Server 2022 or 2025, so replacing the server means the app has nowhere to go.

articles.title: GhostRepo: A Local Autopsy for Abandoned Repositories, with Gemma Doing the Talking
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine Every abandoned repository has a story, but the people who could tell it have usually moved on. What's…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine What I Built Every abandoned repository has a story, but the people who could tell it have usually moved on. What's left is a stale README, a few hundred commits, and a dependency file nobody has touched in years. GhostRepo investigates repositories like these on your own machine and helps you plan their resurrection. Point it at a local repository, choose Summon Ghost , and let it perform an autopsy. Here's what it does: Examines programming languages, frameworks, Git history, dependencies, configuration, documentation, and tests. It also runs Ruff on Python code. Reports verified findings, each backed by evidence, a source file, and its detection method.

In our ongoing quest to develop a moon base, could we possibly utilize the area beneath the surface of the moon in order to make the moon habitable? articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 31, 2015: Creepy skull-shaped Halloween asteroid flies by Earth, NASA names it the 'Great Pumpkin'
articles.excerpt: On October 31, 2015, an asteroid shaped like a human skull flew by Earth. Here's why it was so creepy.
articles.body: On October 31, 2015, an asteroid shaped like a human skull flew by Earth. It arrived with excellent timing on Halloween, which made the already-creepy asteroid even creepier. During its closest approach, the creepy asteroid was about 300,000 miles from Earth, or 1.3 times the average distance between Earth and the moon . So, it didn't pose a threat to our planet. It was discovered by astronomers at Hawaii's Pan-STARRS observatory only three weeks before the flyby, and it was given the official designation "2015 TB145." But no one knew what it looked like until the day before Halloween, when the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico captured the first radar images.

articles.body: The moon dives towards the glowing heart of the constellation Leo for a spectacular rendezvous with Mars and Jupiter overnight on Nov. 1-2, as the glittering stars of the Beehive Cluster shine nearby. Here's what you need to know. Look to the eastern horizon an hour after midnight to see the 45%-lit waning moon shining less than 5 degrees from the red light of Mars — roughly the width of your three middle fingers held at arm's length to the night sky. Jupiter's bright light will gleam just below the red planet, with the bright star Regulus lining up beyond to form a dazzling procession leading back to the horizon. The stars of the Beehive Cluster (M44) can be found twinkling 10 degrees from the unlit side of the lunar disk around this time, in the middle of the constellation Cancer .
